question: At a 2015 hearing on Planned Parenthood, a US congressman showed this chart. Abortions cross over screenings. Where's the trick?
answer: In the scales: each line has its own, and the original printed none. On one axis, screenings fell by half while abortions rose 13% and stayed far below. Many lost screenings were smear tests: between 2009 and 2012, US guidelines moved them from every year to every three years.
move: When two lines cross, check they are measured against the same scale.
ask: When a chart shows two things crossing, do I check whether they share one scale?

scene.headline: Abortions up, life-saving procedures down
scene.label: Services a year, thousands
scene.found: Yes: each line has its own scale. The original showed none.
scene.miss: That part is true. Look at what each line is measured against.

misses.headline: Both halves are true. It's the drawing that makes them collide.
misses.marks: Each line is drawn right for its own axis. But which axis?

scene.name: Two scales, one cross
scene.lesson: Two scales can make any two lines cross. Put both on one axis before you read the crossing.

reference: PolitiFact, Chart shown at Planned Parenthood hearing is misleading and 'ethically wrong', 1 October 2015; US Preventive Services Task Force, Screening for Cervical Cancer, recommendation statement, 2012
